messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Emily is a 28-year-old police officer who lives with her partner in a mid-sized American city. For the past fourteen months, she has been haunted by an event she cannot fully claim as her own. It happened late on a night shift when she was still a probationary officer, riding with her training officer—a man she had trusted to teach her the job, someone she had come to see as a mentor. During what should have been a routine vehicle stop, the driver became combative, and her training officer, instead of backing her up, turned on her. He pinned her against the patrol car, slammed her head against the window, and later told internal affairs that she had escalated the situation. No one questioned him. The official report made it look like she had panicked and that he had restrained her. She was reassigned to a quieter precinct, but the damage was done. What Emily remembers most vividly is the shock of his betrayal—the moment she realized the person meant to protect her was the one causing harm. Her mind stores that instant in full, overwhelming sensory detail: the cold pressure of the glass against her cheek, the smell of his cheap cologne and coffee breath, the grinding sound of her radio as it was crushed beneath his weight. When the memory comes back, and it does constantly, it feels completely real across every sense at once. She has lost count of the mornings she has woken up disoriented, convinced she is still on that street corner. And yet, even as the memory feels that real, it also feels like it belongs to someone else—a stranger she is watching from far away. That hollow contradiction terrifies her more than the violence itself.

Over the months that followed, Emily’s body began to act as if it had its own agenda. Her heart pounds at a distant siren, at a raised voice on a radio call, at the sight of a stationary patrol car with its doors open. She has come to believe that her body is a traitor, forever reacting as if she is still pinned against that window, even when she is standing safely in her own kitchen. Every physiological surge feels like proof that danger is imminent, and that belief has spread outward: the world now seems saturated with threat. She scans every driver she pulls over for concealed anger, every fellow officer for signs of hidden malice. The station house, once a place of camaraderie, now feels like a minefield. She no longer eats lunch in the breakroom because she cannot shake the certainty that someone is watching her, waiting for her to slip. She has stopped socializing with colleagues entirely, and her relationship with her partner has become strained—she flinches when he touches her from behind, she cannot explain why, and she has started sleeping in the guest room because the nightmares jolt her awake screaming.

Emily’s avoidance has become a full-time project. She requested permanent day shifts so she would not have to drive past the intersection where it happened. She deleted the training officer’s contact, unfriended everyone who might mention him, and she has not stepped into the precinct that originally housed her patrol unit in more than a year. The consequences have accumulated quietly: her supervisors have noted her repeated refusal to partner with certain veteran officers, and her performance reviews now include remarks about “difficulty trusting team members.” She knows she is seen as difficult, but the alternative—being vulnerable again—feels unthinkable.

What finally brought Emily to seek help was a moment at work last week. A new officer, young and eager, asked her for advice during a traffic stop. His posture was relaxed, his voice friendly, and Emily suddenly saw her former training officer’s face superimposed on his. She froze, her finger hovering over her radio, drenched in sweat, unable to speak. The officer asked if she was okay, and she stammered an excuse and walked away. That evening, she told her partner she could not keep living this way. She is terrified that her body will betray her at a critical moment—that she will freeze when someone needs her help. She hopes, more than anything, that she can learn to trust her own senses again, and to believe that the danger is not still happening right now.
